title: Problem Overview and References
content: Erdős Problem #811 asks: for which graphs $G$ (with $m = e(G)$ edges) does every balanced $m$-coloring of $K_n$ contain a rainbow copy of $G$? A balanced coloring requires each vertex to see exactly $\lfloor(n-1)/m\rfloor$ edges of each color, which forces $n \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$. A rainbow copy uses all $m$ edge colors distinctly. The problem was posed by Erdős, Pyber, and Tuza (1991) and sits at the intersection of anti-Ramsey theory and extremal graph theory. Recent breakthroughs: Clemen-Wagner (2023) showed $K_4$ fails, and Axenovich-Clemen (2024) extended this to infinitely many complete graphs.
mathContext: For which $G$ with $m = e(G)$ edges: $\forall$ large $n \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$, $\forall$ balanced $m$-colorings $\chi$ of $K_n$, $\exists$ rainbow copy of $G$ in $\chi$?

title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib's simple graph infrastructure, finite set operations, and general tactics. The namespace `Erdos811` isolates all definitions. `open Finset` brings finite set notation into scope for cardinality computations and filtering operations used in color degree definitions.
mathContext: Uses `SimpleGraph (Fin k)` for graph structures and `Finset.univ.filter` for counting

title: Complete Graph Edge Count
content: `completeEdgeCount n` computes $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$, the number of edges in $K_n$. This is used to determine the number of colors needed for balanced colorings of complete graphs: a balanced $m$-coloring of $K_n$ uses $m = \binom{k}{2}$ colors when testing the rainbow property of $K_k$.

title: Edge Coloring Structure and Color Degree
content: `EdgeColoring n m` is a structure assigning a color in `Fin m` to each pair of vertices in $K_n$, with symmetry ($\chi(u,v) = \chi(v,u)$) and irreflexivity (diagonal entries are fixed). `colorDegree χ v c` counts the edges of color $c$ incident to vertex $v$ by filtering over all neighbors. This forms the foundation for the balanced coloring definition.

title: Balanced Coloring and Existence
content: `IsBalanced χ` requires every vertex to see exactly $\lfloor(n-1)/m\rfloor$ edges of each color. This is the key structural constraint: it prevents trivial avoidance strategies where one color class is deliberately sparse. The axiom `balanced_existence` asserts that balanced colorings exist whenever $n \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$ — the divisibility condition ensures $(n-1)/m$ is an integer, so 'balanced' means exactly equal, not just approximately equal.
mathContext: $\chi$ is balanced $\iff \forall v, \forall c: \deg_c(v) = \frac{n-1}{m}$; exists when $m \mid (n-1)$

title: Graph Embedding and Rainbow Copy
content: `GraphEmbedding G n` is an injective map from $V(G)$ into $\text{Fin}\,n$. `IsRainbow G χ emb` asserts that distinct edges of $G$ receive distinct colors under the embedding — i.e., the restriction of $\chi$ to the image of $G$ is injective on edges. `ContainsRainbow G χ` existentially quantifies over embeddings. The injectivity requirement on the embedding is essential: without it, a 'copy' could collapse vertices, violating the graph structure.
mathContext: $G \hookrightarrow K_n$ is rainbow under $\chi$ $\iff$ $\chi$ restricted to $E(G)$ is injective: $\{e_1, e_2\} \subseteq E(G),\, e_1 \neq e_2 \Rightarrow \chi(e_1) \neq \chi(e_2)$

title: The Rainbow Property
content: `HasRainbowProperty G m` formalizes the central concept: $G$ has the rainbow property if there exists $N_0$ such that for all $n \geq N_0$ with $n \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$, every balanced $m$-coloring of $K_n$ contains a rainbow copy of $G$. This is an 'eventually for all' quantifier structure. The problem asks to characterize which graphs $G$ satisfy this.
mathContext: $G$ has the rainbow property $\iff \exists N_0,\, \forall n \geq N_0$ with $m \mid (n-1)$: every balanced $\chi$ of $K_n$ contains a rainbow $G$

title: K₄ Fails: Clemen-Wagner (2023)
content: The axiom `clemen_wagner_2023` formalizes the breakthrough result that $K_4$ does NOT have the rainbow property: for arbitrarily large $n \equiv 1 \pmod{6}$, there exist balanced 6-colorings of $K_n$ with no rainbow $K_4$. This resolved the simplest open case negatively. The number 6 comes from $|E(K_4)| = \binom{4}{2} = 6$. The construction likely uses algebraic or probabilistic methods to create colorings that systematically avoid rainbow 4-cliques while maintaining balance.
mathContext: $\forall N_0,\, \exists n \geq N_0$ with $6 \mid (n-1)$: $\exists$ balanced $\chi$ of $K_n$ with $\nexists$ rainbow $K_4$ in $\chi$

title: Axenovich-Clemen (2024) and Their Conjecture
content: The axiom `axenovich_clemen_2024` extends Clemen-Wagner: infinitely many complete graphs $K_m$ (with $m \geq 4$) fail the rainbow property. The definition `AxenovichClemenConjecture` goes further, conjecturing that ALL $K_m$ with $m \geq 4$ fail. If true, the only complete graphs with the rainbow property would be $K_2$ (trivially, a single edge) and $K_3$ (a triangle, where rainbow = proper coloring, and balanced 3-colorings of $K_n$ always contain properly colored triangles).
mathContext: $\forall K,\, \exists m \geq K$ with $m \geq 4$: $\neg\text{HasRainbowProperty}(K_m, \binom{m}{2})$; conjecture: $\forall m \geq 4$

title: Quantitative Version: Rainbow Minimum Degree
content: The quantitative version introduces $d_G(n)$, the minimum color degree threshold guaranteeing a rainbow copy of $G$. `rainbowMinDegree` is axiomatized as a function. The Erdős-Tuza bounds for $C_4$ give $\lfloor n/6 \rfloor \leq d_{C_4}(n) \leq (1/4 - c)n$. The gap between $n/6 \approx 0.167n$ and $(1/4 - c)n < 0.25n$ shows the threshold is known only up to a constant factor. This quantitative refinement connects to Turán-type density questions.
mathContext: $d_{C_4}(n)$: min color degree forcing rainbow $C_4$; $\frac{n}{6} \leq d_{C_4}(n) \leq \left(\frac{1}{4} - c\right)n$

title: Erdős's Specific Challenge: C₆ or K₄ in 6-Colorings
content: `ErdosChallenge` formalizes Erdős's specific question: in any balanced 6-coloring of $K_{6n+1}$, must there exist a rainbow $C_6$ or rainbow $K_4$? Since Clemen-Wagner showed the $K_4$ part fails, the question reduces to: does every balanced 6-coloring contain a rainbow $C_6$? The axiom `erdos_challenge_K4_false` captures this partial resolution. The disjunction 'rainbow $C_6$ or rainbow $K_4$' is interesting because both graphs have 6 edges, so both use the same number of colors.
mathContext: $\forall$ large $n$, $\forall$ balanced $\chi$ of $K_{6n+1}$ with 6 colors: $\chi \supseteq$ rainbow $C_6$ or $\chi \supseteq$ rainbow $K_4$? ($K_4$ part: NO)

title: Small Cases: Trees and Stars Have the Rainbow Property
content: Two axioms capture positive results: `trees_have_rainbow_property` (any tree $T$ on $k$ vertices has the rainbow property with $k-1$ colors) and `stars_rainbow` ($K_{1,m}$ has the property with $m$ colors). Trees are the simplest connected graphs, and their acyclicity makes the rainbow condition easier to satisfy — there are no closed walks that could create color conflicts. Stars are the most extreme trees (diameter 2), and their star structure means rainbow = injective coloring of edges at one vertex.
mathContext: Trees: $\text{HasRainbowProperty}(T, k-1)$ for all trees $T$ on $k$ vertices; Stars: $\text{HasRainbowProperty}(K_{1,m}, m)$

title: Main Theorem: erdos_811 (OPEN Problem Summary)
content: The main theorem `erdos_811` packages the two key negative results as a conjunction: (1) $K_4$ fails the rainbow property (Clemen-Wagner 2023), and (2) infinitely many $K_m$ fail (Axenovich-Clemen 2024). The proof is a clean pair construction `⟨clemen_wagner_2023, axenovich_clemen_2024⟩`. The problem remains OPEN: the full characterization of graphs with the rainbow property is unknown, and the Axenovich-Clemen conjecture (all $K_m$ fail for $m \geq 4$) is unresolved.
